title: Mad Solutions and Haitham Dabbour’s Irth Platform Announce Strategic Pan-Arab Content Partnership in Venice
description: Pan-Arab distributor Mad Solutions and Egyptian multihyphenate Haitham Dabbour’s Irth platform dedicated to supporting standout writers across the A
body:
Pan-Arab distributor Mad Solutions and Egyptian multihyphenate Haitham Dabbour’s Irth platform dedicated to supporting standout writers across the Arab world announced a strategic partnership on Saturday at the Venice Film Festival that aims to boost quality content output from the region.

	Under the pact, Mad Solutions and Irth will jointly “develop, package and support film, television and other entertainment projects from across the Arab world for regional and international markets,” they said in a statement.
	

	The Irth platform initiative – that was officially launched during the 2025 Red Sea International Film Festival in Saudi Arabia – is the first collaborative writers’ room bringing together writers from Egypt and Saudi Arabia and beyond.


	Cairo-based Mad Solutions, which was established in 2010 by its two co-founders, Alaa Karkouti and Maher Diab, comprises a network of specialized outfits that include Mad World, focussed on international sales of Arab films; Mad Distribution, which handles sales and distribution of Arab films across the Arab world; and Mad Celebrity, providing full talent management and representation for both on-and off-screen Arab talent.

	MAD Solutions and Irth are now developing a pipeline spanning original Arabic projects, some of which are talent-driven, as well as third-party development and consultancy assignments. The first projects germinated from the partnership will be announced, they said.

	The partnership announcement comes just as Mad Solutions marks a significant presence in Venice this year, with two films launching on the Lido. “Al Baraneya,” a rural Egyptian family’s story directed by Egypt’s Ashgan El-Hamus, screening in Venice Days, and Palestinian drama “Conversations with the Sea,” directed by Muayad Alayan, screening in the Venice Spotlight section. 
	

	MAD will also present its annual award at the Final Cut in Venice platform, which supports films from Africa and the Arab world through post-production and international industry opportunities.

	Dabbour is a bestselling Egyptian author whoser novels include “Devoured by Seven Lean Cows” and “Moses Cross.” His screenwriting credits include Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival prizewinner “Gunshot” and “The Tale of Ahl El Daye,” which in 2025 had its European bow in the Berlinale’s Generation section.

	“Irth has always been about bringing strong writers and different Arab voices together and giving ideas the development they need,” Dabbour in a statement. “Mad’s regional and international reach gives us the opportunity to take that work further and open new possibilities for the projects and writers we work with.”

	Commented Mad Solutions co-founders Alaa Karkouti and Maher Diab: “Development is a key part of Mad’s regional and international expansion, and Irth brings a strong creative infrastructure and a diverse network of Arab writers to that strategy. Together, we can originate projects while also offering filmmakers and producers the development support they need to strengthen existing ones.”

schema.headline: Mad Solutions and Haitham Dabbour’s Irth Platform Announce Strategic Pan-Arab Content Partnership in Venice

title: Lav Diaz Preps False Prophets Film and Jose Rizal’s ‘Noli Me Tangere’ Adaptation, Unpacks Venice Title ‘Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Lav Diaz is developing a film about false prophets and a screen adaptation of José Rizal’s “Noli Me Tangere,” the Filipino auteur reveals, alongside
body:
Lav Diaz is developing a film about false prophets and a screen adaptation of José Rizal’s “Noli Me Tangere,” the Filipino auteur reveals, alongside details on “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” (“Makikiraan Po”), his Spanish colonization drama premiering in the Venice Open section of the Venice Film Festival.

	Diaz tells Variety, “Right now, I’m working on a film that discourses on false ideologies and false prophets.” He is also developing a separate project drawing on the writing of “Noli Me Tangere,” the Rizal novel credited with helping inspire the Philippine Revolution of 1896.
	

	Diaz shared those plans alongside a discussion of “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors,” which marks a return to Venice for the director. He won the festival’s Golden Lion in 2016 for “The Woman Who Left.” He arrives with the film following “Magellan,” which stars Gael Garcia Bernal as the Portuguese explorer and premiered at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival.


	“Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” marks Diaz’s third excursion into a specific historical epoch, following “A Lullaby to the Sorrowful Mystery,” anchored in the Philippine Revolution of 1896. This time, Diaz reaches further back, to the late 16th century and early 17th century, when Spanish forces under Miguel Lopez de Legazpi consolidated colonial rule after Legazpi’s 1565 arrival in Cebu, 44 years after Magellan first landed in the archipelago. Chieftain Rajah Tupas resisted the Spanish for nearly a month before Legazpi bombarded local villages, forcing Tupas into a settlement.

	“It is an essential part of my continuing studies and dissection of my people’s struggle, or simply trying to understand the history of the Philippines,” Diaz says.
	

	The film centers on the forced labor used to build the Philippines’ colonial-era churches, structures Diaz argues are steeped in violence despite their standing today as celebrated cultural and religious landmarks. Under Spanish rule, able-bodied Malay men, from teenagers to adults, were required to perform 40 days of unpaid annual labor on roads, bridges, churches, forts, piers, plantations, haciendas and mines.

	“Forgetful Filipinos must learn, must know, must understand, that these structures were built by forced labor, and that they didn’t appear in their midst by some cosmic manifestations — it’s blood, sweat, tears, and deaths of our ancestors,” Diaz says.

	He adds that, based on historical accounts, around 30% of the male population perished under the forced-labor system.

	Diaz extends that critique of institutional power to religion itself. “Religion is one of the worst forms of violence,“ he says. “Faith can be a form of eternal subjugation, especially for the weak. Oftentimes, it blurs all of rationality; it becomes the truth of existence.” He points to the Crusades and the Holocaust as historical examples, and cites present-day conflicts in Gaza, Ukraine, Afghanistan and Darfur as evidence of faith’s continuing entanglement with violence.

	The film’s Filipino title — “Makikiraan Po” — comes from a phrase still used today by Filipino Malays passing through places believed to hold ancestral spirits. “I still do it, naturally, when I am entering a forest, a zone, when I am thinking of the unattainable,” Diaz says. “It is a connection, a relationship, with the ancient, with the primal, the pure.”

	Diaz also traces the roots of the Philippines’ present-day class structure to the encomienda system, which King Philip II ordered Legazpi to impose in 1571. Under the system, indigenous communities lost ownership of their land while paying heavy tributes and performing forced labor for Spanish encomenderos. He says, “All the old rich families, landlords, hacienderos, political clans, big businesses, have their connection from the encomienda.”

	Diaz shot “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” in black and white in Sampaloc, Quezon Province, marking his fourth production in the town, following “Magellan,” “Phantosmia” and the upcoming “Kawalan.” He credits the area with restoring his health after tuberculosis burst his left lung following the editing of “Magellan,” and again after he was later afflicted with severe asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
	

	“The spirit of the place provides the best attributes I needed in my films on issues of truth, vision and transcendence,” he says.

	Diaz cast filmmaker Isabel Sandoval, known for her own distinctive body of work, alongside longtime collaborators Ronnie Lazaro and Yul Servo. Sandoval plays the Babaylan, a traditional Malay healer who Diaz describes as a lasting bridge between Filipinos and their pre-Hispanic, pre-Islamic Malay heritage.

	Diaz says, “She contributed majestic nuance in the whole vision of the Babaylan character, and I am truly grateful for her generosity.”

	At 151 minutes, “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” runs shorter than many of the films Diaz is best known for, though he says his process didn’t change. “Nothing really changed with my praxis,” he says. “My principle has always been to work on the demands of the material at hand, to work around the conditions and situations. There’s never a fixed setup or framework. It’s just all hard work on the different aspects of the process really. The struggle to pursue a vision is the most important.”

	He adds: “Cinema must have the responsibility to commit to the truth. There should be no compromise on that issue given the condition of the world right now. Cinema’s soul is the truth.”

	“Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” is produced by C’est Lovi Prods., Epicmedia Prods. and Sine Olivia Pilipinas, with Heretic handling world sales.

title: As Swiss Films Expand International Reach, English-language Works Are on the Rise
description: Swiss cinema is resonating domestically and abroad as homegrown films and international co-productions continue to entice local audiences and festiv
body:
Swiss cinema is resonating domestically and abroad as homegrown films and international co-productions continue to entice local audiences and festival goers around the globe.

	At Venice this year, Swiss titles and co-productions boasting high-profile talent unspool throughout the festival. Switzerland is also a country of focus at the Venice Production Bridge industry strand with seven projects taking part in the Gap-Financing Market and two in the Immersive Market.
	

	“For a relatively small and multilingual market, the combination of domestic relevance and international reach is significant,” says Nicola Ruffo, director of promotional organization Swiss Films.




	

					‘Who Is Still Alive’
									Courtesy of First Hand Films
	



	“Last year proved that there is a real appetite — fiction, documentaries, films from different linguistic regions and very different kinds of stories all found their audiences. Several of these films also traveled extremely well internationally. Petra Volpe’s ‘Late Shift,’ for example, was a box office success on the domestic market but also sold more than 670,000 tickets outside Switzerland by the end of 2025,” adds Ruffo.

	Venice, Ruffo notes, has in recent years “become a very good snapshot of the vitality of Swiss cinema. We have Swiss films and co-productions appearing across very different parts of the festival. Last year there were the world premieres of ‘Memory of Princess Mumbi’ by Damien Hauser or this year’s Swiss Oscar-entry, ‘Who Is Still Alive,’ by Nicolas Wadimoff, who also received an award in Venice.”



	

					‘The Indies’ 
									Courtesy of Alina Film
	



	Indeed, this year Pauline Julier and Nicolas Chapoulier’s historical drama “The Indies,” from Spain’s Lastor Media and Switzerland’s Alina Film, is competing in Giornate degli Autori, while Wim Wenders’ documentary “From Inside Out — The Architecture of Peter Zumthor,” about one of Switzerland’s most internationally renowned architects, premieres in Venice Open — Out of Competition. The film is produced by Wenders’ Road Movies and German-Swiss shareholding partner DCM group.
	

	In addition, Geneva-based Sunny Independent Pictures is among the producers of Iranian filmmaker Ali Asgari’s main competition title “A Bit of Light,” which centers on a dejected doctor whose suicidal tendencies are checked by his family’s compassion.

	The producers of Venezia Spotlight premiere title “Guria,” Levan Koguashvili’s feature about a stubborn, widowed hazelnut farmer looking to improve his prospects in a Georgian village left destitute by the collapse of the Soviet Union, include Zurich’s Cineworx Filmproduktion, while Gilles Jobin’s “Sunset Motel,” from Geneva’s Nadasdy Film and Cie Gilles Jobin, represents Switzerland in the Venice Immersive competition.

	“What excites me is really the range,” Ruffo stresses. “It is difficult to reduce contemporary Swiss cinema to one aesthetic or a specific topic — and I think that is a strength.”

	Indeed, this year’s Swiss selection at the Venice Production Bridge offers a glimpse of “what may be coming next,” he adds.  

	Among them are works by both up-and-coming and well-established filmmakers such as Flurin Giger, who is developing “A Year Without Summer,” Valentin Merz, who presents “Chocolat Amer,” Stéphanie Argerich with “Kyushu Moon,” Kaveh Bakhtiari, who is developing “The Smuggler,” and Ursula Meier with “Quiet Land.”

	“These are very different filmmakers and projects, many of them working internationally from an early stage, which is precisely what makes the current generation interesting,” Ruffo notes. “There is also an interesting bridge between this emerging generation and established filmmakers who continue to reinvent themselves.“

	Meier’s upcoming “Quiet Land,” for example, is a Swiss-French-Canadian project selected for the Venice Gap-Financing Market that’s set to shoot in North America. “Kyushu Moon,” another Gap-Financing Market title, will lens in Japan, while “The Smuggler” will film in Greece.   

	Ruffo points out that Switzerland is seeing “a continued stream of strong international co-productions” characterized by universal themes.

	“Projects such as ‘Quiet Land’ bring together Switzerland, France and Canada; ‘The Smuggler’ connects Switzerland, Greece and France; and ‘A Year Without Summer’ is Swiss-German.
	

	“At the same time, many of these films remain rooted in very specific places, communities and personal experiences. There is a recurring interest in questions of identity, belonging and how individuals navigate social and cultural boundaries.”

	There is another development that Ruffo finds particularly interesting: “the move toward English-language filmmaking.” At the Venice Production Bridge, Swiss filmmakers Tim Fehlbaum (“September 5“), Ursula Meier and Michael Koch will come together at a panel to discuss precisely this question: What opportunities does work in English create for Swiss directors in terms of international casts, financing and audiences? And what does it mean for the identity of Swiss cinema?



	

					‘Frank & Louis’
									Credit: Rob Baker Ashton
	



	“Michael Koch’s English-speaking debut ‘Erosion,’ with Peter Sarsgaard in the lead role, has entered post-production; Meier’s ‘Quiet Land’ will be shot next year. Petra Volpe received standing ovations in Sundance and just recently won the Locarno audience award for her first English-language film, ‘Frank & Louis’; Denis Rabaglia has a new film, ‘Butterfly Stroke,’ starring Judy Davis, also shot in English, to conquer the international festivals,” says Ruffo, who is not worried about a trend.

	“I do not think becoming more international necessarily means becoming less Swiss. Switzerland has always been multilingual and culturally interconnected. Perhaps our filmmakers are simply taking that reality one step further: telling stories from a particular perspective without allowing language or national borders to define where those stories can travel.

	“So, if I had to describe the direction in a few words, I might say: international, yet unmistakably Swiss. There is a confidence today in moving between languages, countries, formats and disciplines without feeling that this dilutes the identity of the work.”

schema.headline: As Swiss Films Expand International Reach, English-language Works Are on the Rise

title: ‘The Echo Chamber’ Starring Alicia Vikander Seals International Distribution Deals Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “The Echo Chamber,” Andrea Pallaoro’s drama starring Alicia Vikander, Luca Marinelli and Susan Sarandon, has already landed distribution across a ra
body:
“The Echo Chamber,” Andrea Pallaoro’s drama starring Alicia Vikander, Luca Marinelli and Susan Sarandon, has already landed distribution across a raft of key international territories ahead of its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival.

	Paradise City Sales has closed deals for Spain with Vertice360; Australia and New Zealand with Umbrella; Poland with Gutek; Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania with Aero Films; former Yugoslavia and Bulgaria with MCF Megacom; and Taiwan with AV Jet. More territories are under negotiation.
	

	Paradise City Sales is also handling North American sales alongside UTA Independent Film Group. The film will be released in Italy by 01 Distribution, while O’Brother will distribute in Benelux. 


	The film centers on Leo and Anne, whose relationship becomes caught in a cycle of attraction and separation as the boundaries between intimacy and dependence, care and control and presence and absence steadily begin to collapse. Ava’s presence — and particularly her voice — reaches across different layers of the story, bringing buried emotions and memories to the surface.

	“The Echo Chamber” carries autobiographical echoes of Bernardo Bertolucci. The film grew out of a story and screenplay by the late Italian master, together with Ilaria Bernardini and Ludovica Rampoldi; Pallaoro subsequently took on the project and developed the screenplay further with Bernardini and Rampoldi after Bertolucci’s death. 

	The film also has a strong musical component. Sarandon, Marinelli and Vikander all perform songs in the film, whose licensed music also includes tracks by Jamie xx, Marianne Faithfull and Nick Cave, Nina Simone and Imagine Dragons. 
	

	Pallaoro previously attended Venice with “Medeas,” “Hannah” and “Monica.” The latter competed at the festival and earned its star Charlotte Rampling the Volpi Cup for best actress. 

	“The Echo Chamber” was produced by Nicola Giuliano, Francesca Cima, Carlotta Calori and Viola Prestieri for Indigo Film, alongside Paolo Del Brocco for Rai Cinema, with Jacques-Henri Bronckart and Tatjana Kozar producing for Belgian co-producer Versus Production.

title: Spain’s Impulse Cinema and Italy’s Fandango Forge Strategic Partnership to Boost Co-Production and Sales Opportunities (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Spanish indie studio Impulse Cinema and Italy’s Fandango have forged a strategic partnership to boost Spanish and Italian productions through co-pro
body:
Spanish indie studio Impulse Cinema and Italy’s Fandango have forged a strategic partnership to boost Spanish and Italian productions through co-production, financing, distribution and global sales.

	The agreement was announced on Saturday at the Venice Production Bridge, the Venice Film Festival‘s market focused on film production.

	Impulse Cinema, which is headed by Andrés Sánchez Pajares and Roberto Butragueño, is Spain‘s first large-scale integrated indie studio that operates across the entire value chain — from development financing and co-production to international distribution and worldwide sales. 
	

	The Madrid-based company is supported by the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT) under the NextGenerationEU program, under which it has tapped into €8 million ($9.3 million) in funding.


	Impulse Cinema and its studios provide financing, co-production, distribution and international sales services, plus access to state-of-the-art production infrastructure, including image processing laboratories, sound post-production facilities, visual effects services and, of course, soundstages for Spanish and international film and TV projects.

	Domenico Procacci’s Fandango is among Italy’s leading indie film production and distribution companies with more than 100 movies to its credit since it launched in 1989. Fandango is at Venice, in different guises, with five titles, including Nanni Moretti’s “It Happened One Night” and Marco Bechis’ “Back to Buenos Aires,” both in competition.

	Besides involving production, the partnership between Impulse Cinema also covers international distribution of Italian and international films with Impulse participating as a partner, working alongside Fandango Sales on global sales. 
	

	“Today, more than ever, European independent cinema needs new collaborative models to help ambitious projects grow and reach wider international audiences,” said Fandango founder and chief Domenico Procacci in a statement. “By combining our respective expertise and investment capacity, we can offer independent producers stronger support while allowing them to develop their projects with greater autonomy.”

	“This collaboration will create new opportunities for the projects in which Fandango is involved, helping outstanding films fulfil both their artistic ambitions and commercial potential,” he added.

	Sánchez Pajares and Butragueño commented: “Italy is home to one of Europe’s most respected and creative film industries, and Fandango is one of its leading companies. Through this partnership, we aim to build a lasting bridge between our two countries by making our innovative studio model available for outstanding film projects and supporting their international growth. We firmly believe that closer collaboration between producers, distributors and investors across Europe is essential to making our industry more competitive on the global stage.”

schema.headline: Spain’s Impulse Cinema and Italy’s Fandango Forge Strategic Partnership to Boost Co-Production and Sales Opportunities (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Powerfully Moving as Ian Charleson, the ‘Chariots of Fire’ Star Who Played Hamlet While Ravaged by AIDS
description: “Elsinore,” named for Hamlet’s castle, opens on a production of that Shakespeare play at the National Theatre in London — but we see it from the bor
body:
“Elsinore,” named for Hamlet’s castle, opens on a production of that Shakespeare play at the National Theatre in London — but we see it from the bored, amused vantage of the backstage technicians, who get seriously jarred when the doddering actor playing the ghost of Hamlet’s father keeps forgetting his lines, and the actor playing Hamlet gets so pissed off that he stalks off the stage in mid-performance. The year is 1989, and that fiery young actor is Daniel Day-Lewis. (Walking off that stage, never to return to the production, is the first famous thing he did that seemed…extreme.) At first we think: Is this some weird theater biopic in which the young Daniel Day figures in? Yes and no.
	

	The movie is not about him. It’s about another classy, dashing, well-known-at-the-time British actor — Ian Charleson (played by Andrew Scott), who was one of the two stars of “Chariots of Fire,” which had come out eight years before. He played Eric Liddell, the devout Scottish Christian who ran his Olympic races for the glory of God. That movie won the Oscar for best picture, so it placed Charleson, with his blond WASP handsomeness and slightly recessive severity, squarely on the map. As “Elsinore” opens, we see that he’s been trying to make good on it ever since.


	But the sad truth is that Charleson, at 39, is already a has-been. His Hollywood career hasn’t panned out, and wherever he goes, people remember him from “Chariots of Fire,” which has become his badge of shame (and, in the film, something of a running joke), since the thing everyone loves most about that movie is the whooshing romantic synthesizer score by Vangelis. (At one point he gets into a cab, and the driver sings it for him.) They’re not wrong. “Chariots” was a decent movie, but take the music out of it and you’re left with a stiff-upper-lip “Masterpiece Theatre” period sports drama that was not exactly a famously strong best picture winner.
	

	Charleson was a momentary heartthrob, but now, with his two-tone frosted hair (like George Michael’s, or maybe like Day-Lewis’ in “My Beautiful Laundrette”), and his delicate and abashed manner, he’s a gay actor who’s trying to contort himself to fit into the roles he’s offered, which are mostly in trashy B genre movies. Is he in the closet? Not exactly. Out and about in London, in the pubs and discos, he lives a vibrant gay life. Yet he doesn’t broadcast it, because he knows that will hurt him professionally. He’s still trying to maintain a “straight” image in a mostly straight entertainment world. Early in his career, he made a movie called “Jubilee” (1978) with the transgressive gay director Derek Jarman (played here with whiplash ferocity by David Dawson), who is furious at him for having scrubbed that film from his resume.

	So why are we watching a biopic about Ian Charleson? Because in 1989, he did something extraordinary. As we learn early on in “Elsinore,” he’s been diagnosed with HIV, which for him, thus far, has resisted erupting into full-blown AIDS. (He refuses to take AZT, which he considers a lame leftover chemo drug that does nothing.) Each day, he checks out his body with a hand mirror to make sure that there are no Kaposi’s sarcoma lesions. Then, one day, as he’s sitting in the make-up chair getting ready to go onto a movie set, he finds one — a small purple blotch on his right temple. He thinks it’s a death sentence. But karma has other ideas.

	With Daniel Day-Lewis having dropped out of “Hamlet,” the play’s director, Richard Eyre (Johnny Flynn), wants to replace him with Ian. Charleson had played the Prince of Denmark once before (in 1974, when he was just 25, and by his own admission too young for the part). But now he’s ready. It’s the role of a lifetime. But can he play it while dying?

	I put it that starkly because full-blown AIDS, in 1989, was a death sentence, and “Elsinore” is the first movie in a while to take us back to that tragic and haunted era. But since we’re at a very different place now, and the scalding pain (and scandal of government indifference) that defined those years is now a part of our history, “Elsinore” is not trying to be a raw, in-your-face AIDS drama like “Longtime Companion.” Yet the film, written by Stephen Beresford and directed by Simon Stone, has every bit as much on its heart and mind.
	

	“Elsinore” is about the shock and trauma of the AIDS epidemic. It’s about the culture of gay actors who felt compelled to hide their identities not out of shame but out of survival. It’s about the passion, and extraordinary heavy lifting, of performing the most profound and daunting of all of Shakespeare’s plays. And it’s about how all of this comes together in the quietly heroic person of Ian Charleson — who, just at the moment when he needs to be taking supreme care of his health, and not weakening himself by taking on the ultimate demanding theater role (4,167 lines of dialogue! Performed before a nightly audience of 1,100 on the hallowed Olivier stage of the National Theatre), decides that he must take on the role. He does it because it’s the chance of a lifetime, but more than that he does it to live. He does it to embrace the life of the theater, at its most incandescent, as a way to ward off death. And maybe he does it to embrace death too, since “Hamlet,” among other things, is all about death. 

	Andrew Scott, who looks remarkably like Ian Charleson, gives an astonishingly layered and moving performance. His Ian is a man who loves life — the life of a British celebrity, an erotic adventurer, and an actor who’s gifted and ambitious enough to think of himself as an artist. Yet the specter of AIDS hangs over him like the Sword of Damocles. Once the lesions start showing up, you feel how the awareness of the disease colors his mood, as his natural ebullience tries to fight off a crestfallen despair. That battle plays out in the clinic of Margaret Johnson (Olivia Colman), the physician whose care he comes under. She’s ahead of the curve in administering AIDS treatments and feels that she can extend his life. But she’s big on doctor’s orders, and the last thing on earth she thinks that Ian should be doing is playing Hamlet.

	This is no quaint battle. Dr. Johnson is trying to save Ian’s life, and he’s saying, “Fuck that. I don’t care.” The tender power of “Elsinore” is the way that Scott’s performance takes us right inside Ian’s state-of-mind — his belief that what’s left of his life needs to mean something, and that playing Hamlet will give it that meaning. Colman, in stringy auburn hair, makes a crisply delectable antagonist (who is really, of course, on Ian’s side). But it’s the antagonism melting into hard-won communion that passes between Ian and Derek Jarman (who also has AIDS) that is most moving. For what that relationship is really about is the impossible situation these men are trying to navigate — how to be true to their art by being who they really are, even under the gun of overwhelming prejudice. By the end of “Elsinore,” that’s what Ian has done. He has used the role of Hamlet to look death in the face, and to lay bare his soul onstage. “Elsinore” is in many ways styled as an art-house crowd-pleaser, and on that score it faces steeper odds than a film like this one might have a few decades ago. But Andrew Scott makes it an indelible journey.

schema.headline: ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Powerfully Moving as Ian Charleson, the ‘Chariots of Fire’ Star Who Played Hamlet While Ravaged by AIDS

title: Impact of War in Iran Set to Feature in Two Venice Film Festival Dramas
description: With war still ravaging Iran — six months after the country was attacked by U.S. and Israeli forces — the Venice Film Festival is set to launch two
body:
With war still ravaging Iran — six months after the country was attacked by U.S. and Israeli forces — the Venice Film Festival is set to launch two Iranian films that will provide viewers vivid on-the-ground insight on the conflict’s societal impact as the country contends with bombs and its repressive regime.

	Ali Asgari, who was in Venice Horizons last year with dark satire “Divine Comedy,” is set to return to the Lido — this time in competition — with “A Bit of Light,” a drama featuring “The Seed of the Sacred Fig” star Misagh Zareh as a doctor who loses faith in the future after being arrested by Iranian authorities and having his medical practice in Tehran shut down.
	

	“This Trump guy is threatening to bomb here every day,” a person helping the doctor says in a key scene in “A Bit of Light.” “And these window panes are huge. God forbid they should shatter and hurt you.”


	Then there is Mohsen Gharaei’s Horizons player “Falling House,” which follows a modest family on the outskirts of Tehran who face the imminent destruction of their home as part of a vast redevelopment project.

	“Falling House” marks Gharaei’s follow-up to “Blockage,” which portrayed corruption in contemporary Iranian society and won best film at Busan in 2017, before going on to play at Rotterdam and Munich.

	“Both films deal with this feeling of being trapped and what do you do when you’re inside a system where there’s really no way out?” says Oscar-winning producer Odessa Rae (“Navalny,” “The Voice of Hind Rajab”), who is a producer on “Falling House” and also served as an executive producer on “Bit of Light.”
	

	“The regime is a part of the problem, and then the West’s solution becomes the other part of the problem,” adds Rae. “And when you’re faced with no way out, how do you behave? How does it transpire in your family? How does it transpire in the choices you make for yourself?” 

	These timely Iranian films were both shot surreptitiously in Iran in what Rae calls “the country’s final spurt of creativity before being battered by the war.”

	To get permits to shoot “Falling House” in Tehran, the film’s lead producer Milad Khosravi — an Iranian who now runs his Seven Springs Pictures production company out of Istanbul — had to “manipulate the script that we gave to government,” he says. Then, after a roughly 70-day shoot, they got the footage out of Iran just before the war started and did the post-production, and a few additional scenes, in Germany. 

	Khosravi, who is also the lead producer on “A Bit of Light,“ says that when the U.S. first attacked Iran in February, physical production of Asgari’s new film had to be moved outside of the country. “We had a really complex situation shooting the film both in Tehran and Istanbul,” notes Khosravi, who adds that they wanted to “finish the film in a timely manner, so that it could make an impact.”

	“We are happy to be launching both these very important films from the Venice Film Festival, so that we can use this important platform to expose the reality of what is happening in Iran,” says Khosravi.

	Khosravi, Asgari and Gharaei, who are now living in exile outside Iran, will all be in Venice for their films‘’’ bows. But it’s very doubtful that they will be able to promote them in the U.S. due to the country‘s travel bans.

	“I think right now with the current administration it’s going to be very hard to get them visas for the U.S.,” says Rae. Khosravi foresees that he will have the same problem.

	That said, the producers have high hopes that “A Bit of Light” and “Falling House” will get U.S. distribution. CAA Media Finance is handling U.S. rights on “Falling House,” while Paradise City Sales is repping international sales. “A Bit of Light” is being sold globally by Salaud Morisset, which has already clinched deals in several countries including France (Haut et Court), Italy (Teodora Film Distribuzione) and Spain (La Aventura Cine).
	

	Both Rae and Khosravi underline that “there won’t be another film on the scale of ‘Falling House’ coming out of Iran for years,” as Rae puts it. “Everything in Iran has been cracked down on,” she says. 

	“The Iranian cinema industry is big; we have a lot of amazing directors,” says Khosravi. “And I’m trying to bring these kinds of stories outside the country by financing them and supporting them thanks to amazing partners like Odessa. I am trying to keep this bridge between Iranian cinema, and global cinema and financiers and festivals, because I feel a responsibility to keep this cinema alive.”



	

					“Falling House“/Venice Film Festival

title: ‘The Idiot(s)’ Review: Dostoevsky Is an Endearing Drunken Fool in This Rambunctious, Tonally Off-Kilter Two-Hander
description: As biographical films on major historical figures go, “The Idiot(s)” starts off with an advantage over most, since it covers only a finite, conflict
body:
As biographical films on major historical figures go, “The Idiot(s)” starts off with an advantage over most, since it covers only a finite, conflict-laden passage of its subject’s storied life. This enjoyably off-kilter dramedy then further ingratiates itself with viewers bored of traditionalist hagiographies, because it also functions as a biting exercise in separating the art from the artist.

	That’s not precisely with the intention of justifying one’s enjoyment of a creator’s body of work despite their unsavory personal past; on the contrary, the hope is that even as the less flattering characteristics of seminal Russian author Fyodor Dostoevsky are exposed, one can still find value in his perspective. The image of the bearded wise man behind literary landmarks that dissect the human condition is exchanged for that of a wretched gambler, a drunken fool drowning in his childish arrogance, thus deliberately detaching him from the grandeur of his oeuvre.
	

	Here he’s closer to some of his doomed characters than to the polished mirage of intellectual depth on painted portraits and photographs. This Dostoevsky (Johnny Flynn)—made of flesh, blood, vomit and other impolite bodily fluids — and his much younger wife Anna (Aimee Lou Wood) have arrived in Germany on their honeymoon. The famed he accrued with “Crime and Punishment” follows him, yet the pompousness of Western Europe disgusts Fyodor, an insufferably proud Russian. Early on in the film, he out-Russians his compatriot and fellow scribe Ivan Turgeniev (Christian Friedel, “The Zone of Interest”) in an impromptu dance off. The cowardly, devious Turgeniev has assimilated to the comforts of the West —that alone is enough for Fyodor to detest him.
	

	That “The Idiot(s)” is the work of Polish filmmakers Małgorzata Szumowska and Michał Englert, once a married couple whose personal and professional lives have long been intertwined, makes sense of their fashioning the narrative as a two-hander where Anna carries as much dramatic weight as Fyodor, if not more. The filmmaking duo, whose previous collaborations include “Never Gonna Snow Again” and “Infinite Storm,” largely based their tale on Andrew D. Kaufman’s novel “The Gambler Wife: A True Story of Love, Risk and the Woman Who Saved Dostoyevsky.”

	Throughout the financial troubles that the couple face given Fyodor’s inability to deliver pages, Szumowska and Englert feature scatological humor that further dissolves any notions of elegance associated with 19th-century Europe. Instead, “The Idiot(s)” highlights the contrast between the palatial accommodations of the elite and the grimy apartments where Fyodor and Anna must reside while he attempts to complete the manuscript for “The Idiot.” The depravity of the aristocrats in the periphery comes off as deliciously cartoonish, likely because that’s how Fyodor perceives them. One of them in particular, portrayed with vicious snark by Vicky Krieps, revels in the moral decay of her times, thirsting for blood.

	When Fyodor is asked by the rich to share a salacious personal anecdote for their entertainment, he takes the opportunity to tell a tale of class and sorrow that transfixes his audience. Not only does he showcase his storytelling prowess but simultaneously unmasks their out-of-touch mentality. In a visceral performance under a prominent beard, Flynn tackles Dostoevsky with an unabashed proclivity for debauchery and a lack of self-control that often render him a puddle of humiliation and desperation. When Fyodor drags himself on the floor, begging for forgiveness or a bit more money to play roulette, the gesture straddles the line between humor and intense discomfort — veering into cringe comedy.

	The wonderful Wood, meanwhile, infuses Anna with open-hearted charisma and cleverness, securing the balance in their onscreen relationship. Making backdoor deals to secure they don’t starve and picking up Fyodor’s slack in more ways than one, Wood’s Anna emerges as an unassuming force who seems to put up with more than she should. And yet, when Szumowska and Englert portray Fyodor’s reaction to the couple’s pregnancy, the birth of their child, and a subsequent tragedy, Anna’s adoration for this utterly flawed man almost feels justified.
	

	Anna, the film suggests, admires her husband warts and all, perhaps because there’s an enticing authenticity in all his inadequacies and brutish ways. Theirs is an unconventional romance, where she must accept his belief in suffering and precariousness as the raw material for the pages that she transcribes for him. Amid a duel, a suicide, a nightmare decapitation to punish misogyny, and all manner of rowdy behavior, “The Idiot(s)” holds on to the promise that a new timeless masterwork can be born from a year of madness, so long as one person, Anna, never stops trusting that her partner can do so. She gets all the credit here, deservingly.  

	The anachronistic use of A-ha’s “Take on Me” in a pared-down version, minus the electronic beat, is typical of the playfulness with which the filmmakers retell the events. If all that’s come before didn’t assure the viewer that they had no airs of solemn, rigorous fatefulness, the recognition of a timeless track from another period might land as an amusing sonic wink. From our modern vantage point, it’s easy to think of those who defined culture centuries ago as stiff characters in antiquated formal clothing with concerns distant from our own. However, the bold absurdism of “The Idiot(s),” tucked inside an impeccably produced costume drama, demystifies those assumptions; the film makes the case for bringing revered entities down from their pedestal and into the arena of quotidian woes and vices. Their work could be even more revelatory in the aftermath.

title: Venice: ‘My Undesirable Friends’ Director on Epic Documentary About Death of Press Freedom in Russia, How Putin’s Crackdown Is Warning for U.S.
description: If her epic, Oscar-shortlisted documentary “My Undesirable Friends: Part 1 — Last Air In Moscow” pulled off an astonishing feat, chronicling the las
body:
If her epic, Oscar-shortlisted documentary “My Undesirable Friends: Part 1 — Last Air In Moscow” pulled off an astonishing feat, chronicling the last gasps of press freedom in Vladimir Putin’s Russia in real time, docmaker Julia Loktev somehow manages to raise the stakes in the film’s arresting sequel.

	Premiering out of competition in the Venice Open strand of the Venice Film Festival, “My Undesirable Friends: Part 2 — Exile” offers a remarkable bookend to its predecessor. Following “Last Air’s” subjects in the aftermath of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Loktev offers an intimate portrait of journalists under threat as they flee their homeland and attempt to rebuild their shattered lives abroad.
	

	Speaking to Variety over Zoom, Loktev unpacks the relationship between the two films while insisting the second part is “a much more complex story.” 


	“It takes place over four and a half years versus four and a half months,” she says. “And it’s a much more emotional story. It’s people who have had to leave their country on a moment’s notice.” 

	Beginning in the fall of 2021, the first chapter of Loktev’s documentary epic charted the months leading up to the Ukraine invasion. Part two begins just two days later with her subjects in flight, some leaving Moscow within hours of learning that their employer, TV Rain, the independent news station that had been designated an “undesirable organization” by the Kremlin, was set to be raided by the police.

	The New York-based Loktev, who was born in the former Soviet Union but emigrated to the U.S. as a child with her family, admits that she didn’t expect the documentary she’d set out to make five years ago would become so Tolstoyan in scope, ultimately spanning nearly 12 hours across 10 chapters. (Part 2 will screen in Venice with an intermission.) 
	

	The director initially planned to chronicle a group of independent journalists who had been declared “foreign agents” by the Russian government. Looking back, Loktev says, “I had absolutely no idea that I [would be] capturing history.” 

	Several months after filming began, Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine. Independent media, already imperiled due to the Kremlin’s crackdown on dissent, was all but outlawed. Effectively branded enemies of the state, the journalists whose lives she documented in “Last Air in Moscow” scattered across Europe and the U.S., with Loktev filming “Exile” as they settled into new lives from Istanbul to Amsterdam, from Prague to New York.

	It was, Loktev says, a “strange nomadic existence.” Armed with little more than her trusted iPhone X, she captures her subjects at their most unguarded, revealing moments of fear, vulnerability and, above all, courage as they navigate what she describes as the new “normal not normal” of their lives.

	It will be difficult for American audiences to watch “My Undesirable Friends” and not see echoes of our country’s own rightward tilt during this Trump presidency, even though Loktev began filming “deep in the Biden era.” “It seemed very far away,” she says, of the second Trump administration and its sweeping assaults against civil liberties. 

	In a scene from the film, one of her protagonists shares a message she composed to her younger self: “Stay alarmed, be hysterical if you need to, and know that it’s very easy to lose your country.” 

	It’s a warning echoed by Loktev. 

	“We have to be very aware of the fear where we internalize the pressures. Where you don’t say something you could have said. Where you don’t do something you could have done,” she says. “I think we’re all plenty anxious now….Hopefully that doesn’t become an anxiety that is paralyzing. It should be an anxiety that is mobilizing.”

title: Venice Immersive Celebrates 10 Years of XR Evolution and the Growth of Location-Based Entertainment
description:
Ten editions in, Venice Immersive has plenty to celebrate — just don’t expect the new-media showcase to spend much time looking back.

	“We’re not p
body:
Ten editions in, Venice Immersive has plenty to celebrate — just don’t expect the new-media showcase to spend much time looking back.

	“We’re not planning any retrospectives,” Venice Immersive counselor Michel Reilhac says of this year’s landmark edition. “Instead, we want to focus on what’s happening next. This really feels like the beginning of a second chapter, for us and for the wider medium.”


	Still, it’s impossible to mark the milestone without taking stock. What launched in a modest nook between two floors of the Palazzo del Casinò now occupies its own island in the lagoon — evolving from festival curiosity into a key hub for a protean art form.
	

	The industry’s progress, meanwhile, has been anything but linear. The long-awaited consumer boom in personal headsets never quite materialized. Project financing from platforms and hardware makers contracted sharply as a result, and (mostly European) public funding stepped in as a bridge — though global profitability is now increasingly coming from elsewhere, as event-based spaces and collective exhibition models prove viable on their own terms.

	“The location-based entertainment (LBE) model now drives the market,” says counselor Liz Rosenthal. “In Asia especially, we’ve seen an explosion of LBE centers built for scale, showcasing projects designed for groups of six, eight, 10 people up to hundreds, depending on the space. The storytelling and design have gotten far more sophisticated, too. In the past you weren’t really embodied as a character, and you couldn’t interact with objects or people. That’s changed.”
	

	Competition titles like “Amsterdam 1652: The Hands of the City,” “Smithsonian Starstruck: An Immersive Experience” and “Everest: The First Ascent” embody that shift, bringing free-roam, multiplayer experiences to educational and heritage venues. Their partners lend a degree of stability — and, increasingly, new sources of financing. “Smithsonian Starstruck,” for instance, was funded by Fever, the leading marketing and ticketing platform for immersive experiences worldwide.

	“New models are starting to emerge,” Rosenthal says. “With Fever, we’re seeing private investment with distribution attached — they’re putting money into the production while also bringing the ticketing, marketing and audience infrastructure to the table.”

	New actors are even rethinking existing models as immersive productions keep taking new shapes. In a certain light, the music experience “Bowie: Unseen | Unheard” could be seen as an artistic showcase underwritten by a hardware manufacturer eager to demonstrate its latest technology. Only here, that company is speaker maker L-Acoustics, and the project does away with headsets entirely — redefining immersive LBE around spatial sound.

	“Sound is art, and we mean to showcase that,” says L-Acoustics exec Amber Mundinger. “It’s incredibly important to show the possibilities of how experiences can be delivered at the highest level of quality. A purpose-built space like the one created for Venice can be replicated around the world, giving people the same unique experience. The goal is to keep it intimate, with 20 to 30 people at a time living inside Bowie’s world while staying sonically true each time. That’s where LBE is heading.”

	Indeed, the 30 projects selected for this year’s Venice Immersive competition illustrate just how far the ecosystem has expanded beyond tech. The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation is backing “Empire at Sea,” while human rights organization B’Tselem makes its first foray into production with “Raj’in (We Shall Return),” a 360-degree documentary following three Palestinian families in the West Bank. National film funds and co-production partners, meanwhile, have adapted traditional film-financing structures for XR — even turning arthouse éminences grises like Abderrahmane Sissako (“Artou”) into immersive evangelists.
	

	For her part, director Hilde K. Kjøs is helping guide new institutional players into the fold. The filmmaker and photographer discovered VR during the pandemic, escaping lockdown through her headset and quickly getting hooked. She channeled that passion into “Finding Frida,” which casts the work of 19th century textile artist Frida Hansen into a dreamlike world. Notably, the project is also the first XR title supported by the Norwegian Film Institute.

	“The film is about the importance of role models,” says Kjøs. “We hope it can show the way for other filmmakers coming from documentary and 2D, so we’re treating it more like a pilot than a prototype, effectively running out ahead, building structures and sharing knowledge about everything from pipelines to international distribution, so that the system can catch up. They can take a chance once, but the Norwegian Film Institute and other funders need to see projects succeed in order to come back and fund more.”



	

					“Finding Frida”
	



	The lineup:

	Projects featuring David Bowie, Daisy Ridley, Margot Robbie and Isabelle Huppert bring plenty of star power to this year’s Venice Immersive. But the festival’s biggest draw may turn out to be a pair of glasses that weigh next to nothing.

	Enter the XREAL Aura, Google-powered AR smart glasses being positioned as a potential jolt for a sluggish headset market.

	“These glasses overcome one of the main hurdles to global access,” says Venice Immersive counselor Michel Reilhac. “Previous VR headsets have always felt clunky and heavy. Now you get similar definition, color and contrast in something streamlined, lightweight, easy to carry and wear. They will define the next decade.”

	Capitalizing on the buzz, festival organizers have partnered with Agog — the XR institute co-founded by Wendy Schmidt — to run a four-day “petting zoo,” where festivalgoers and industry delegates can drop in, no reservation required, to test the hardware. The Immersive competition will also feature two experiences built for the device: Andy Serkis’s “Nevatars,” starring Daisy Ridley, and the Margot Robbie-hosted “Galápagos: The Last Eden.”

	“Most of what we’ve seen until now has been data- or sound-driven demos,” Reilhac says. “Whereas these two are fully fledged spatial narratives, with sophisticated storytelling and AI-driven voice activation that lets you talk directly to the characters. The magic is having that level of aesthetic and sonic quality in an ordinary pair of glasses. That’s a new wow effect.”
	

	For “Galápagos” director Anthony Geffen, interactivity is the real breakthrough.

	“You have to play to the medium’s strengths,” he says. “You’re not just watching Margot Robbie take you through the islands — you can reach out, engage with the world and see how the animals have changed. We even built a digital Darwin you can turn to at any point, and he’ll answer questions about his time there or anything else you want to know. That’s what makes this different from film, television or gaming.”

	The abundance of boldface talent attached to this year’s projects is no accident. In a medium still defining its own identity, star appeal is a strategic.

	“We’re still in Immersive’s Méliès or Edison era,” says industry veteran Peter Flaherty. “We’re building the grammar and syntax for an undefined art form — figuring out how to tell a story for eight to ten people at once, in an amorphous participatory experience, without alienating the audience. That’s why casting matters.”

	For “Empire at Sea” — an AR drama that threads climate science into a propulsive narrative — Flaherty chose familiarity over megawatt fame, betting that veteran character actors like Orlando Jones and Beth Grant would do a better job onboarding viewers.

	“That subconscious effect of recognizing someone without necessarily placing them makes the audience more comfortable with the storytelling,” Flaherty says. “It makes the experience less uncanny. Overall, leaning into familiarity is exactly where we need to be.”

            An Illinois mother is accused of murdering her 2-year-old son hours after texting friends about the Lindsay Clancy trial.
      
    
            38-year-old Corie Walsh was initially hospitalized but then moved to a jail.
      
    
            Corie was arrested after cops came to her home on Tuesday. Officers arrived to find a 17-year-old neighbor giving the young child CPR. Law enforcement rushed the toddler to the hospital, where officials said he died.
      

            The neighbor said he found Corie in a room of the home harming herself. The incident came hours after Corie was chatting it up in a group text about the Lindsay Clancy murder case. 
      
    
            Prosecutors claim Corie told them she murdered her son because he was the devil. The police found a second young kid in the home, but he was unharmed. The two children’s father was not present. 
      
    
            The Will County Coroner’s Office ruled the child died by homicide. The cause of death has yet to be determined.

title: Burning Man Attendee Dies After Medical Emergency at Nevada Festival
description:
Burning Man
                          Participant Dies at Festival
body:
Burning Man
                          Participant Dies at Festival
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A man is dead after suffering a medical emergency at the Burning Man festival in Nevada.
      
    
            Organizers say the man, who was in his mid-50s, became sick Thursday at the Black Rock Desert event. He was treated with lifesaving measures before being transported to the festival's emergency care center, where he was pronounced dead.
      
    
            The death comes as heavy rain forced officials to close the festival's main entrance and exit gate. Organizers urged people planning to attend to delay their travel ... while those already at the event were told to avoid driving.
      
    
            The incident also comes one year after the death of 37-year-old Vadim Kruglov, who was found fatally stabbed inside a tent at Burning Man in August 2025.
      
    
            Kruglov’s death was considered the first recorded homicide in the festival's history.
